claim: Twenty-eight rats were trained in a one-drop sucrose intensity discrimination task.
source: Twenty-eight rats were trained in a one-drop sucrose intensity discrimination task.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the behavioral experiments.

claim: Trained rats initiate a trial by first visiting the central port.
source: Trained rats initiate a trial by first visiting the central port (Return).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the trial structure.

claim: Licking at the central spout triggers the delivery of either 10 µL of 3 (Low) or 18 (High) wt% sucrose.
source: Licking at the central spout triggers the delivery of either 10 µL of 3 (Low) or 18 (High) wt% sucrose (referred to as Cue-D; Stimulus).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the trial structure.

claim: If a rat chooses correctly by moving to one of the two lateral ports, three drops of water are delivered as a reward.
source: If a rat chooses correctly (by moving to one of the two lateral ports; Response), three drops of water are delivered as a reward (Outcome).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the trial structure.

claim: Error trials were unrewarded.
source: Error trials were unrewarded.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the trial structure.

claim: Subjects achieved the learning criterion (≥80% correct) in about 25 sessions.
source: Subjects achieved the learning criterion (≥80% correct) in about 25 sessions (Figure 1B)
evidence: Stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1B showing performance across training days.

claim: The implantation of an electrode array in one of the three cortical areas did not impair task performance.
source: and the implantation of an electrode array in one of the three cortical areas did not impair task performance (paired t-test before vs. after surgery; t(27) = 0.95; p=0.35; Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with statistical test results and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: In generalization sessions, rats were required to classify 0, 3, 4.75, 7.5, 11.75, or 18 wt% sucrose as either 'Low' or 'High'.
source: In these sessions that consisted of 20% of the trials, rats were required to classify 0, 3, 4.75, 7.5, 11.75, or 18 wt% sucrose as either 'Low' or 'High' (referred as Cue-G).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing generalization sessions.

claim: In generalization trials, no reward was delivered to avoid imposing an arbitrary Low/High threshold that could bias the behavioral report of the perceived sweetness intensity.
source: In these trials, no reward was delivered (Reward omission) to avoid imposing an arbitrary Low/High threshold that could bias the behavioral report of the perceived sweetness intensity.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing generalization trials.

claim: In Cue-G trials the percentage of 'High' responses increased with increasing sucrose concentration.
source: In Cue-G trials the percentage of 'High' responses increased with increasing sucrose concentration (Figure 1D)
evidence: Stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1D showing psychometric function.

claim: The animals used sucrose intensity as a cue to solve the task since its quality is unchanged.
source: thus showing that the animals used sucrose intensity as a cue to solve the task (since its quality is unchanged (Pfaffmann et al., 1979)).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with citation to support that sucrose quality is unchanged.

claim: Surgery did not impair perceptual judgments based on sucrose intensity.
source: Surgery did not impair perceptual judgments based on sucrose intensity (see Before vs. After surgery; Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1D comparing psychometric functions before and after surgery.

claim: The latency to stop licking after High Cue-D delivery (18% sucrose) was longer (0.74 ± 0.02 s) than for the Low Cue-D (3% sucrose; 0.58 ± 0.01 s; p < 0.0001).
source: the latency to stop licking after High Cue-D delivery (18% sucrose) was longer (0.74 ± 0.02 s) than for the Low Cue-D (3% sucrose; 0.58 ± 0.01 s; p < 0.0001).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: Rats exhibited a longer time to stop licking in trials where sucrose intensities were ≥to 4.75% relative to Low Cue-D.
source: A similar trend was observed for generalization cues (i.e., Cue-G trials), in that rats exhibited a longer time to stop licking in trials where sucrose intensities were ≥to 4.75% relative to Low Cue-D (One-way ANOVA: F(7,1360) = 17.10; p < 0.0001; Dunnett post-hoc; Figure 1E).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with statistical test results and supported by Figure 1E.

claim: Rats lick more rhythmically and similarly for both cues in sessions where their performance was better.
source: Furthermore, we analyzed the relationship between licking and task performance and found that rats lick more rhythmically and similarly for both cues in sessions where their performance was better.
evidence: Stated in the Results section based on analysis of licking behavior.

claim: There is a positive correlation between Low and High licking PSTHs and task performance (r = 0.17, p < 0.003).
source: This is reflected by a positive correlation between Low and High licking PSTHs and task performance (r = 0.17, p < 0.003; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with statistical test results and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rats did not solve the task by licking differently for both cues.
source: Thus, rats did not solve the task by licking differently for both cues.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the licking analysis.

claim: In the Return epoch, rightward movements (left to center port direction) were faster than leftward (right to center port) movements.
source: In the Return epoch, rightward movements (left to center port direction) were faster than leftward (right to center port) movements (Figure 1F).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1F.

claim: During the Response epoch, leftward or rightward movements were not significantly different.
source: In contrast, during the Response epoch, leftward or rightward movements were not significantly different (Figure 1G)
evidence: Stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1G.

claim: Movements in the Response and Return epochs were independent of the sucrose concentration.
source: and therefore these movements were independent of the sucrose concentration.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a conclusion from movement analysis.

claim: Rats moved faster in the Response than in the Return period, perhaps a result of the water reward.
source: Interestingly, rats moved faster in the Response than in the Return period, perhaps a result of the water reward (compare Figure 1F vs. Figure 1G).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with speculative reasoning and supported by Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Rats rapidly detected when the reward was omitted.
source: Finally, in the Outcome epoch, rats rapidly detected when the reward was omitted (Cue-G trials and Cue-D error trials).
evidence: Stated in the Results section based on licking behavior analysis.

claim: Rats spent more time licking when water was delivered than when it was omitted.
source: That is, they spent more time licking when water was delivered than when it was omitted (Figure 1H; see Supplementary file 1 for statistics).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with reference to statistics and supported by Figure 1H.

claim: By using only a 10 µL drop of sensory stimulation, rats can make accurate perceptual decisions based on the perceived concentration of sucrose.
source: In sum, by using only a 10 µL drop of sensory stimulation, rats can make accurate perceptual decisions based on the perceived concentration of sucrose.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a summary conclusion from behavioral experiments.

claim: A total of 1348, 1169, and 1010 single-units were recorded from pIC, aIC, and OFC, respectively.
source: A total of 1348, 1169, and 1010 single-units were recorded from pIC, aIC, and OFC, respectively (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the Electrophysiology section with reference to figure.

claim: Of the neuronal responses, 480, 403, and 337 from pIC, aIC, and OFC respectively were recorded in generalization sessions.
source: Of these neuronal responses 480, 403, and 337, respectively were recorded in generalization sessions and the rest in discrimination sessions (with only cue-D trials).
evidence: Directly stated in the Electrophysiology section.

claim: Recordings were performed unilaterally in the left hemisphere.
source: Recordings were performed unilaterally in the left hemisphere.
evidence: Directly stated in the Electrophysiology section.

claim: Most recorded neurons exhibited a statistically significant evoked response: 90.6% (1221/1348), 97.4% (1139/1169), and 92.8% (937/1010) for the pIC, aIC, and OFC, respectively.
source: Most recorded neurons exhibited a statistically significant evoked response 90.6% (1221/1348), 97.4% (1139/1169), and 92.8% (937/1010) for the pIC, aIC, and OFC, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing modulation profiles.

claim: The remaining neurons, named Non-evoked, were 9.4% (127/1348), 2.6% (30/1169), and 7.2% (73/1010) for pIC, aIC, and OFC respectively.
source: The remaining neurons, named Non-evoked, were 9.4% (127/1348), 2.6% (30/1169), and 7.2% (73/1010), respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing modulation profiles.

claim: Cue-evoked responses were classified according to five characteristic modulation profiles: Phasic, Tonic-Inactive (Inact), Tonic-Active (Act), Lick-coherent Inactive (Coh-Inact), and Active (Coh-Act).
source: Cue-evoked responses were then further classified according to five characteristic modulation profiles: Phasic, Tonic-Inactive (Inact), Tonic-Active (Act), Lick-coherent Inactive (Coh-Inact), and Active (Coh-Act) (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing modulation profiles.

claim: ~95% of recorded neurons were responsive to a single drop of sucrose (Cue-D).
source: We found that ~95% of recorded neurons were responsive to a single drop of sucrose (Cue-D)
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section summarizing findings.

claim: The majority of responsive neurons were unable to distinguish between 3 and 18 wt% sucrose.
source: but the majority of them were unable to distinguish between 3 and 18 wt% sucrose.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section summarizing findings.

claim: The massive number of responsive neurons could be the result of the arrival of a salient cue (Cue-D) to an over trained animal.
source: We posit that such a massive number of responsive neurons, which includes Intensity-selective and Non-selective neurons (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), could be the result of the arrival of a salient cue (Cue-D) to an over trained animal.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of findings.

claim: The stimulus is highly relevant in the context of thirsty subjects whose internal state would motivate them to attend to the delivery of a stimuli whose accurate detection and identification will lead to obtaining water.
source: This stimulus is highly relevant in the context of thirsty subjects whose internal state would motivate them to attend to the delivery of an stimuli whose accurate detection and identification will lead to obtaining water.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of findings.

claim: A state of physiological need (e.g., hunger) gates insular cortex responses to food cues.
source: These findings are in agreement with observations that a state of physiological need (e.g., hunger) gates insular cortex responses to food cues (Livneh et al., 2017)
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: Caudolateral OFC neurons are sensitive to hunger.
source: and that caudolateral OFC neurons are sensitive to hunger (Rolls et al., 1989).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: In head-fixed trained mice, odor stimulation triggers a massive widespread cortical activation in mice performing a Go/No-Go goal-directed behavior.
source: Likewise, in head-fixed trained mice, it was recently reported that odor stimulation also triggers a massive widespread cortical activation in mice performing a Go/No-Go goal-directed behavior (Allen et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: Electrophysiological studies in rodents and non-human primates have reported a low proportion (ranging between 2–35%) of Insular (pIC) and OFC neurons with selective responses to at least one taste quality.
source: For example, electrophysiological studies in rodents and non-human primates have reported a low proportion (ranging between 2–35%) of Insular (pIC) and OFC neurons with selective responses to at least one taste quality (Pritchard et al., 2005; Rolls et al., 1990; Rolls et al., 1989; Scott et al., 1991; Stapleton et al., 2006; Thorpe et al., 1983; Yamamoto et al., 1989; Yaxley et al., 1990).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: One recent study in anesthetized mice, using a calcium sensor (GcAMP6), reported almost 90% of taste responses in the pIC were tastant selective although only 26% were sucrose-best.
source: In contrast, one recent study in anesthetized mice, using a calcium sensor (GcAMP6), reported almost 90% of taste responses in the pIC were tastant selective although only 26% were sucrose-best (Fletcher et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: In the monkey Insula cortex, Scott et al. (1991) found that less than 1.5% (24/1661) of the recorded neurons responded linearly to increasing glucose concentrations.
source: In this regard, in the monkey Insula cortex, Scott et al. (1991) found that less than 1.5% (24/1661) of the recorded neurons responded linearly to increasing glucose concentrations.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: This data is the first demonstration that a small subset of cortical neurons represents sucrose intensity better than the entire population.
source: To the best of our knowledge, our data is the first demonstration that a small subset of cortical neurons represents sucrose intensity better than the entire population.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a novel finding.

claim: Intensity-selective neurons comprise 18% of neurons in a rat's cortex, which would represent a large population.
source: Although intensity-selective neurons comprise a 'small' population relative to Non-selective neurons (Figure 3B and Table 2), we note that 18% of neurons in a rat's cortex would represent a large population.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of findings.

claim: Intensity-selective neurons were present in the recorded three cortical regions.
source: In this regard, it is interesting that Intensity-selective neurons were present in the recorded three cortical regions.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section summarizing findings.

claim: Experiments in the mouse Insula cortex show the existence of non-overlapping posterior (aversive-pIC) and anterior (appetitive-aIC) 'hotspots'.
source: This result is somewhat surprising in light of the experiments in the mouse Insula cortex showing the existence of non-overlapping posterior (aversive-pIC) and anterior (appetitive-aIC) 'hotspots' (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: Gain and loss of function experiments in mice have demonstrated that the 'sweet hotspot' is sufficient and necessary for sweet taste recognition.
source: Gain and loss of function experiments in mice have demonstrated that the 'sweet hotspot' is sufficient and necessary for sweet taste recognition (Peng et al., 2015)
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: A similar topographic separation of disgust-appetitive in monkeys' anterior Insula has been found, although in a different anatomical axis (dorsal–appetitive and ventral-aversive).
source: and a similar topographic separation of disgust-appetitive in monkeys' anterior Insula has been found, although in a different anatomical axis (dorsal–appetitive and ventral-aversive (Jezzini et al., 2012)).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: Sucrose's identity is initially encoded in the sweet hotspot (located in aIC), but information about its perceived intensity is then distributed to other areas.
source: One explanation for the distributed responses that we observed (Figures 2 and 3) is that sucrose's identity is initially encoded in the sweet hotspot (located in aIC), but information about its perceived intensity is then distributed to other areas.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation for findings.

claim: Each of the three cortical regions contains information about sucrose intensity, revealing the distributed nature of taste intensity coding.
source: Nevertheless, we found that each recorded cortical region decoded sucrose intensity equally well, including the pIC which according to (Chen et al., 2011) is where the 'aversive hotspot' is located. Thus, whatever the explanation, each of these three cortical regions contains information about sucrose intensity, revealing the distributed nature of taste intensity coding.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from findings.

claim: The fact that all three areas decoded sucrose intensity equally well does not imply that they represent the same information, but rather they may encode different features of the sucrose intensity cues.
source: However, the fact that all three areas decoded sucrose intensity equally well does not imply that they represent the same information, but rather they may encode different features of the sucrose intensity cues.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of findings.

claim: The pIC should play a general role in gustation since it receives most inputs from the gustatory thalamus.
source: In this regard, and despite that stimulation of the pIC elicits aversive behavioral responses (Peng et al., 2015), we posit that the pIC should also plays a general role in gustation since it receives most inputs from the gustatory thalamus (Cechetto and Saper, 1987), which could rationalize why there is sucrose responses in this cortical area (Fletcher et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The aIC responses might be related to encoding the sweet percept, due to the 'sweet' hotspot, whose activation leads to appetitive behaviors.
source: The aIC responses might be related to encoding the sweet percept, due to the 'sweet' hotspot, mentioned above, whose activation leads to appetitive behaviors (Chen et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The OFC responses during the Stimulus epoch could signal the relative reward value of Low and High sucrose cues.
source: Finally, the OFC responses during the Stimulus epoch could also signal the relative reward value of Low and High sucrose cues (Rolls et al., 1990; Tremblay and Schultz, 1999).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The perceived intensity of sucrose is spatially distributed along taste cortices with a compact and distributed neural code.
source: Our data suggest that the perceived intensity of sucrose is spatially distributed along taste cortices with a compact and distributed neural code, in the sense that a small subset of spatially disperse neurons contain more information, about sucrose intensity, than the entire population (Field, 1994; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Stüttgen et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from findings with citations.

claim: Additional information about sucrose's intensity was conveyed in the spike timing of neurons.
source: In this regard, we found that additional information about sucrose's intensity was conveyed in the spike timing of neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to figure.

claim: A recent study in the olfactory system reported that piriform cortex neurons encode odor intensity by using only the spike timing, and not the spike count information.
source: A recent study in the olfactory system reported that piriform cortex neurons encode odor intensity by using only the spike timing, and not the spike count information (Bolding and Franks, 2017).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: Spike count is also a contributor to encoding taste intensity since Sensory neurons tracked the concentration of sucrose by increasing its firing rate.
source: However, spike count is also a contributor since we found Sensory neurons that tracked the concentration of sucrose by increasing its firing rate (Figure 4).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to figure.

claim: In the taste system, both spike count and spike timing information could be complementary codes for the perceived intensity of sucrose.
source: Thus, in the taste system, it seems that both spike count and spike timing information could be complementary codes for the perceived intensity of sucrose.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from findings.

claim: Precise spike timing entrained by rhythmic licking serves as an internal clock, relevant for coordinating activity across brain regions.
source: Precise spike timing entrained by rhythmic licking serves as an internal clock, relevant for coordinating activity across brain regions (Gutierrez et al., 2010; Gutierrez et al., 2006; Roussin et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The Lick-Coherent neurons were both sufficient and necessary to decode the perceived intensity of sucrose.
source: We found that the Lick-Coherent neurons were both sufficient and necessary to decode the perceived intensity of sucrose (Tables 3 and 4).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to tables.

claim: The level of coherence was significantly higher in the Stimulus-epoch in comparison with the pre-Stimulus and the Outcome epochs.
source: More importantly, we also uncovered, for the first time, that the level of coherence was significantly higher in the Stimulus-epoch in comparison with the pre-Stimulus and the Outcome epochs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to figure.

claim: Lick-spike coherence not only reflects oromotor responses, but is also involved in gating the input of sensory and taste information that can be 'read out' across taste cortices in coordination with licking.
source: This result implies that lick-spike coherence not only reflects oromotor responses, but that it is also involved in gating the input of sensory and taste information that can be 'read out' across taste cortices in coordination with licking (Buzsáki, 2010; Gutierrez et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: A distinct subset of neurons exhibited Choice-related activity in aIC and OFC with responses that covaried with the subject's choices.
source: We found that a distinct subset of neurons exhibited Choice-related activity in aIC and OFC with responses that covaried with the subject's choices (Figure 5).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to figure.

claim: OFC (but not aIC) neurons tracked choice before a response was emitted.
source: Furthermore, OFC (but not aIC) neurons tracked choice before a response was emitted.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section summarizing findings.

claim: Behavioral observations suggest the subjects have already made a decision before leaving the central port.
source: These findings are in agreement with behavioral observations which suggests the subjects have already made a decision before leaving the central port (Perez et al., 2013; Uchida and Mainen, 2003).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The findings reveal a neural correlate of the perceived intensity of sucrose in the gustatory system.
source: Our findings reveal a neural correlate of the perceived intensity of sucrose in the gustatory system.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from findings.

claim: OFC neurons robustly encoded movement direction.
source: In this regard, here we also found that OFC neurons robustly encoded movement direction.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section summarizing findings.

claim: Neurons with direction selectivity in the OFC have been recorded in tasks involving two or four spatial locations.
source: Likewise, neurons with direction selectivity in the OFC have been recorded in tasks involving two or four spatial locations (Feierstein et al., 2006; Lipton et al., 1999; Roesch et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Lesioning the OFC disrupts performance in an allocentric foraging task.
source: Lesioning the OFC disrupts performance in an allocentric foraging task (Corwin et al., 1994), and radial arm and Morris water maze (Kolb et al., 1983).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The OFC encodes head angle, spatial trajectory and movement speed in a spatial discrimination and reversal task in a plus maze.
source: Moreover, the OFC also encodes head angle, spatial trajectory and movement speed in a spatial discrimination and reversal task in a plus maze (Riceberg and Shapiro, 2017).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: Ablating either the pIC or the aIC results in a severe impairment of spatial navigation in a water maze.
source: In contrast, less is known about the participation of the Insular Cortex in encoding spatial navigation parameters; although, it is known that ablating either the pIC or the aIC results in a severe impairment of spatial navigation in a water maze (Nerad et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: For the first time, neurons in the pIC and aIC tracked movement direction.
source: Here, for the first time, we found that neurons in the pIC and aIC tracked movement direction, probably through their connections with the entorhinal cortex (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a novel finding with citation.

claim: According to the Pindex values, the encoding of direction was weaker in the IC in comparison to the OFC.
source: However, according to the Pindex values, the encoding of direction was weaker in the IC in comparison to the OFC (Figure 6).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to figure.

claim: The data points to a dominant role for the OFC, and to a lesser extent the IC, in encoding movement direction.
source: Altogether, our data points to a dominant role for the OFC, and to a lesser extent the IC, in encoding movement direction; an essential feature of spatial navigation for goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from findings.

claim: Previous observations have shown that aIC and OFC neurons encode reward omission.
source: Previous observations have shown that aIC and OFC neurons encode reward omission (Feierstein et al., 2006; Jo and Jung, 2016)
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The pIC, aIC, and the OFC differentially respond to the presence and absence of reward.
source: and we found the pIC, aIC, and the OFC differentially respond to the presence and absence of reward (Figure 7); suggesting a distributed tracking of reward omission.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to figure.

claim: This is the first demonstration that pIC neurons could also encode reward omission.
source: However, this is the first demonstration that pIC neurons could also encode reward omission.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a novel finding.

claim: The pIC has a key role in updating the current outcome representation to guide action selection.
source: The pIC has a key role in updating the current outcome representation to guide action selection. This is because without affecting the execution of the instrumental responses its chemogenetic inhibition impairs the ability of subjects to adjust their actions based upon the outcome current value (Parkes et al., 2018; Parkes et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The results demonstrate a widespread representation of neural signals related to the Outcome, which is a crucial process for learning and adaptive behavior.
source: Our results demonstrate a widespread representation of neural signals related to the Outcome, which is a crucial process for learning and adaptive behavior.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from findings.

claim: The main similarity among all three brain regions was that they decoded sucrose concentration equally well.
source: The main similarity among all three brain regions was that they decoded sucrose concentration equally well.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section summarizing findings.

claim: A major difference was that OFC neurons carry information about decision-variables earlier and with higher quality than neurons in the Insula.
source: A major difference was that OFC neurons carry information about decision-variables earlier and with higher quality than neurons in the Insula (Figures 5–7).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to figures.

claim: Unlike the Insula, the OFC was the brain region with more neurons jointly encoding more than one decision-variable (Choice, Direction, and Outcome).
source: That is, unlike the Insula, the OFC was the brain region with more neurons jointly encoding more than one decision-variable (Choice, Direction, and Outcome; Figure 8A), indicating that the OFC has a complete representation of the most relevant task events.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to figure.

claim: The OFC provides an up-to-date representation of task-related information that is required to yield the best outcome.
source: It follows that the OFC provides an up-to-date representation of task-related information that is required to yield the best outcome.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of findings.

claim: In reinforcement learning, this information is named 'state' representation.
source: In reinforcement learning, this information is named 'state' representation (Schuck et al., 2018; Stalnaker et al., 2016; Sutton and Barton, 1998).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The OFC is involved in encoding the subjective reward value of associated choices.
source: The OFC is also involved in encoding the subjective reward value of associated choices (Conen and Padoa-Schioppa, 2015; Rolls, 2004; Tremblay and Schultz, 1999).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: In the task, correct actions (choosing left/right) led to the same reward (i.e., 3 drops of water).
source: However, in our task correct actions (choosing left/right) led to the same reward (i.e., 3 drops of water)
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section describing the task design.

claim: OFC neurons could encode spatiomotor variables, such as Choice and Movement direction, even for actions with the same reward value.
source: suggesting, in agreement with findings in an odor guided task (Feierstein et al., 2006), that OFC neurons could encode spatiomotor variables, such as Choice and Movement direction, even for actions with the same reward value.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: OFC may act as a hub that represents decision-variables regardless of the type of sensory input used to guide goal-directed behaviors.
source: We posit that OFC may act as a hub that represents decision-variables regardless of the type of sensory input used to guide goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of findings.

claim: The OFC is a brain area well suited to perform this function since it receives connections from sensory areas related to olfactory, gustatory, visual, and somatosensory processing.
source: The OFC is a brain area well suited to perform this function since it receives connections from sensory areas related to olfactory, gustatory, visual, and somatosensory processing (Cavada et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: In animals trained to identify sucrose intensity the taste system uses a compact and distributed code to represent its perceived intensity.
source: We found evidence that in animals trained to identify sucrose intensity the taste system uses a compact and distributed code to represent its perceived intensity.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a concluding remark.

claim: The perceived intensity of sucrose and the decision-variables associated with the discrimination task can be fully reconstructed from a small population of neurons in the pIC, aIC, and OFC.
source: Moreover, the perceived intensity of sucrose and the decision-variables associated with the discrimination task can be fully reconstructed from a small population of neurons in the pIC, aIC, and OFC.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a concluding remark.

claim: Sucrose evoked a widespread response in neurons recorded in posterior-Insula (pIC), anterior-Insula (aIC), and Orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
source: We trained rats in a sucrose intensity discrimination task and found that sucrose evoked a widespread response in neurons recorded in posterior-Insula (pIC), anterior-Insula (aIC), and Orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
evidence: Stated in the Abstract summarizing main findings.

claim: Only a few Intensity-selective neurons conveyed the most information about sucrose's intensity.
source: Remarkably, only a few Intensity-selective neurons conveyed the most information about sucrose's intensity, indicating that for sweetness the gustatory system uses a compact and distributed code.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract summarizing main findings.

claim: For sweetness the gustatory system uses a compact and distributed code.
source: Remarkably, only a few Intensity-selective neurons conveyed the most information about sucrose's intensity, indicating that for sweetness the gustatory system uses a compact and distributed code.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a conclusion from findings.

claim: Sucrose intensity was encoded in both firing-rates and spike-timing.
source: Sucrose intensity was encoded in both firing-rates and spike-timing.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract summarizing main findings.

claim: Sucrose's sweet intensity is one attribute contributing to the overconsumption of high-energy palatable foods.
source: Sucrose's sweet intensity is one attribute contributing to the overconsumption of high-energy palatable foods.

source: However, it is not known how sucrose intensity is encoded and used to make perceptual decisions by neurons in taste-sensitive cortices.

claim: Chemical stimulation of taste receptor cells elicits signals that are transduced into neural representations of multiple attributes, such as taste quality, intensity, and palatability.
source: Chemical stimulation of taste receptor cells elicits signals that are transduced into neural representations of multiple attributes, such as taste quality, intensity (the strength or concentration of a stimulus), and palatability (hedonic value).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as background information.

claim: These attributes form a single percept that informs the animal whether it is safe to ingest the food.
source: These attributes form a single percept (Accolla et al., 2007; Breslin, 2013; Lemon, 2015) that informs the animal whether it is safe to ingest the food (Tapper and Halpern, 1968).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Sucrose is the prototypical highly palatable tastant for sweet taste quality, and it provides a sensory cue predicting the presence of immediate energy sources.
source: Sucrose is the prototypical highly palatable tastant for sweet taste quality, and it provides a sensory cue predicting the presence of immediate energy sources.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as background information.

claim: Wang et al., 2018 found that palatability and intensity do not always change together and suggested that they are two distinct representations.
source: Although palatability and intensity usually change together, Wang et al., 2018 found this is not always the case and suggested that they are two distinct representations.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: In rodents, palatability is measured by an increase in positive oromotor responses (e.g., licking) elicited by increasing sucrose concentrations.
source: In rodents, palatability is measured by an increase in positive oromotor responses (e.g., licking) elicited by increasing sucrose concentrations (Spector and Smith, 1984).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: The intensity attribute cannot be directly measured by any licking response per se, as an animal must actively report the perceived concentration of sucrose, a process necessarily involving decision-making.
source: In contrast, the intensity attribute cannot be directly measured by any licking response per se, as an animal must actively report the perceived concentration of sucrose, a process necessarily involving decision-making.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as background information.

claim: Historically, the neural representation of sweet taste intensity has been characterized by firing rates (spike counts) that monotonically increase with sucrose concentration along the gustatory pathway from the periphery to primary (IC) and secondary (OFC) taste cortices.
source: Historically, the neural representation of sweet taste intensity has been characterized by firing rates (spike counts) that monotonically increase with sucrose concentration along the gustatory pathway from the periphery to primary (IC) and secondary (OFC) taste cortices (Rolls et al., 1990; Roussin et al., 2012; Scott et al., 1991; Thorpe et al., 1983; Villavicencio et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Those responses were obtained in either anesthetized animals, during passive intraoral delivery of tastants, or in behavioral tasks where animals do not have to make any decision other than to lick.
source: However, those responses were obtained in either anesthetized animals (Barretto et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015), during passive intraoral delivery of tastants (Maier and Katz, 2013; Scott et al., 1991), or in behavioral tasks where animals do not have to make any decision other than to lick (Rosen and Di Lorenzo, 2012; Stapleton et al., 2006; Villavicencio et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The neural representation of the perceived intensity of sucrose that the animal actively reports has not presently been studied.
source: Thus, the neural representation of the perceived intensity of sucrose that the animal actively reports has not presently been studied.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as the research gap.

claim: How this representation is transformed into perceptual decision-variables, such as choice, movement direction, and the presence or absence of reward remains to be elucidated.
source: Likewise, how this representation is transformed into perceptual decision-variables, such as choice, movement direction, and the presence or absence of reward remains to be elucidated.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as the research gap.

claim: The three cortical areas (pIC, aIC, OFC) are multimodal and chemosensitive and are involved in disgust (pIC), tastant identification (aIC), and subjective value and reward (OFC).
source: These three cortical areas are multimodal and chemosensitive and are involved in disgust (pIC), tastant identification (aIC), and subjective value and reward (OFC) (Frank et al., 2013; Gardner and Fontanini, 2014; Jezzini et al., 2013; Jones et al., 2006; Katz et al., 2001; Kusumoto-Yoshida et al., 2015; Maffei et al., 2012; Maier and Katz, 2013; Verhagen et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In rodents, the pIC has been shown to be involved in taste, disgust, expectancy, and aversive motivated behaviors.
source: In rodents, the pIC has been shown to be involved in taste, disgust, expectancy, and aversive motivated behaviors (Bermúdez-Rattoni, 2004; Chen et al., 2011; Fletcher et al., 2017; Gardner and Fontanini, 2014; Gutierrez et al., 2010; Kusumoto-Yoshida et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The aIC is involved in appetitive behaviors, and besides having neurons that respond selectively to sweet taste, it also has neurons encoding reward probability and reward omission.
source: In contrast, the aIC is involved in appetitive behaviors, and besides having neurons that respond selectively to sweet taste (Chen et al., 2011), it also has neurons encoding reward probability and reward omission (Jo and Jung, 2016).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Both pIC and aIC have roles in taste and decision-making, but their contribution to sucrose intensity guided behavior remains unexplored.
source: Even though both pIC and aIC have roles in taste and decision-making, their contribution to sucrose intensity guided behavior remains unexplored.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as the research gap.

claim: OFC is involved in reward and subjective value.
source: It is well known that OFC is involved in reward and subjective value (Conen and Padoa-Schioppa, 2015; Jo and Jung, 2016; Kennerley and Wallis, 2009; Roesch et al., 2006)

claim: OFC is a critical brain region for encoding decision-variables such as choice, movement direction, and reward omission.

evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: It is not known whether OFC neurons encode decision-variables guided by sucrose intensity.
source: However, it is not known whether OFC neurons encode decision-variables guided by sucrose intensity.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as the research gap.

source: Equally unknown is how these variables are encoded along the posterior-anterior axis of the Insula.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as the research gap.

source: 82% of the evoked responses showed no selectivity to sucrose intensity, whereas 18% could be labeled as sucrose intensity-selective.

claim: Intensity-selective neurons conveyed the most information about sucrose's sweet intensity.
source: These selective neurons conveyed the most information about sucrose's sweet intensity.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction summarizing findings.

claim: Analyses of the sucrose-evoked responses revealed that, in addition to firing rates, the spike timing of neurons contains additional information about sucrose's intensity.
source: Analyses of the sucrose-evoked responses revealed that, in addition to firing rates, the spike timing of neurons contains additional information about sucrose's intensity.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction summarizing findings.

claim: The three recorded areas similarly decoded sucrose concentration and equally tracked the outcome (reward delivery or omission).
source: Overall, the three recorded areas similarly decoded sucrose concentration and equally tracked the outcome (reward delivery or omission).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction summarizing findings.

claim: The OFC neurons carry information about behavioral choice and movement direction, earlier and with higher quality than neurons in the Insula.
source: A major difference among them was that the OFC neurons carry information about behavioral choice and movement direction, earlier and with higher quality than neurons in the Insula.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction summarizing findings.

claim: The perceived intensity of sucrose is fully reconstructed from the firing rate and spike timing of a small population of neurons in the pIC, aIC, and OFC.
source: In summary, these data show that the perceived intensity of sucrose is fully reconstructed from the firing rate and spike timing of a small population of neurons in the pIC, aIC, and OFC.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as a concluding statement.

claim: 45.1% of all Intensity-selective neurons have a 'best-window' with no differences in licking.
source: We found that 45.1% of all Intensity-selective neurons have a 'best-window' (interval with maximal discrimination between concentrations) with no differences in licking (see Figure 2 grey-line above the PSTHs).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with reference to figure.

claim: The remaining 54.9% of neurons have a lick rate difference inside the best-window, but most frequently they only covered a small fraction of the window.
source: The remaining 54.9% of neurons have a lick rate difference inside the best-window, but most frequently they only covered a small fraction of the window (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with reference to figure.

claim: The overlap of the lick rate differences covered 31.4% of the entire best-window.
source: Specifically, the overlap of the lick rate differences covered 31.4% of the entire best-window (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with reference to figure.

claim: It is unlikely that most sucrose intensity representation can be attributed to differences in licking behavior.
source: Thus, we conclude that is unlikely that most sucrose intensity representation can be attributed to differences in licking behavior.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a conclusion from analysis.

claim: The pIC (60.3%) and aIC (59.5%) had a higher proportion of lick-induced oscillatory responses than the OFC (27.6%).
source: In line with previous studies (de Araujo et al., 2006; Gutierrez et al., 2010), we found among these taste cortices that the pIC (60.3%) and aIC (59.5%) had a higher proportion of (either increasing or decreasing) lick-induced oscillatory responses than the OFC (27.6%).

claim: The coherence values of the OFC (0.24 ± 0.005) were significantly lower relative to pIC (0.26 ± 0.003) and aIC (0.26 ± 0.003).
source: Likewise, we found that the coherence values of the OFC (0.24 ± 0.005) were significantly lower relative to pIC (0.26 ± 0.003) and aIC (0.26 ± 0.003) (F(2, 1672)=3.77; p = 0.02) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).

source: Therefore, the pIC and aIC had not only a higher proportion of Lick-coherent neurons than OFC, but also IC neurons were better entrained with rhythmic licking.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a conclusion from analysis.

claim: The contribution of the Non-evoked responses was found to be at chance level (50%), indicating that they contained little, if any, information about sucrose intensity.

claim: All Cue-D evoked neuronal responses (All- black bars) significantly decoded sucrose concentrations above chance level.
source: In contrast, all Cue-D evoked neuronal responses (All- black bars) significantly decoded sucrose concentrations above chance level (Figure 3B).

claim: The small population of Intensity-selective neurons (red bars) contained more information than the larger Non-selective population (blue bars).

evidence: Stated in the Results section with reference to figure.

claim: The Non-selective group also decoded sucrose intensity significantly above chance level.
source: Interestingly, the Non-selective group also decoded sucrose intensity significantly above chance level.
evidence: Stated in the Results section.

source: When the spike timing information was eliminated from these neuronal responses, their ability to decode among the sucrose's intensities dropped to chance level (Figure 3B; see the horizontal white lines across the blue bars).

claim: The additional information in the Non-selective population was likely conveyed by precise spike timing patterns of activity.
source: Thus, the additional information in the Non-selective population was likely conveyed by precise spike timing patterns of activity.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a conclusion from analysis.

claim: The Intensity-selective neurons in the three cortical regions decoded sucrose intensity better than Non-selective neurons.
source: The decoding algorithm also revealed that the Intensity-selective neurons in the three cortical regions decoded sucrose intensity better than Non-selective neurons (Figure 3B; red bars).

source: It has been reported that spike counts in a pair of simultaneously recorded neurons, elicited by a stimulus, can covary across the session, a phenomenon denominated as noise-correlation and these correlations are thought to covary with attentional, behavioral, and overall brain-state of the network (Averbeck et al., 2006).
